auditor_notes: Content fetched live from Supabase. Factual verification via SikhiToTheMax, SikhiWiki, Wikipedia (Guru Granth Sahib, Ten Gurus, Five Ks, Khalsa, Amrit Sanskar, Bandi Chhor Divas, Naam Karan, Akhand Path, Nishan Sahib), Britannica. GGS 305:4 cross-checked via sikhitothemax.org (content confirmed as Gauri raag section; the specific sub-verse citation is plausible for early-morning worship context but not directly verifiable from web results alone — flagged as LOW). Web search cap ~35/40 used.

findings.lesson_title: The Nature of God and the Mool Mantra

issues.claim_in_lesson: The Mool Mantra opens with the numeral 1 — in Punjabi script, Ik Onkar — followed by a series of attributes. The Mool Mantra teaches that God is: one (Ik Onkar); the Truth (Sat Nam — whose name is truth); the Creator (Karta Purakh); without fear (Nirbhau); without enmity (Nirvair); beyond time and death (Akal Murat); self-existent (Ajooni Saibhang); and known through the grace of the Guru (Gur Prasad).
issues.verdict: Substantially correct. The transliterations match the standard Romanised forms used in GCSE teaching. 'Ajooni Saibhang' is one accepted rendering of 'Ajuni Saibhang'. No material error.
issues.note: The lesson cites GGS 1a as the location of the Mool Mantar — this is accurate (Ang 1 of the GGS). Minor: some scholarly sources end the Mool Mantar at 'Gur Prasad' while others include the following salok; the lesson does not take a position on this debate, which is fine for GCSE level.

issues.claim_in_lesson: Sikhism is one of the world's youngest major religions, founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab region of South Asia in the late fifteenth century.
issues.verdict: Correct. Guru Nanak was born in 1469 and his public ministry began c.1499–1500, placing the founding firmly in the late fifteenth century. Phrasing is accurate.

issues.claim_in_lesson: When Guru Nanak emerged from the River Bein after three days in what Sikhs believe was a direct encounter with God, his first words were: 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.'
issues.verdict: Accurate account per Janamsakhi tradition. 'Three days' is the standard version; some accounts say 'three days and nights'. No error.

findings.overall_lesson_verdict: PASS — no HIGH or MEDIUM issues found. Mool Mantar attributes, GGS citation, founding date, Ik Onkar monotheism, immanence/transcendence distinction, Waheguru etymology all accurate.

findings.lesson_title: Human Life, Sikh Virtues and Mukti

issues.claim_in_lesson: 1. Dharam Khand 2. Gyan Khand 3. Saram Khand 4. Karam Khand 5. Sach Khand
issues.verdict: Correct order and names. These are the five khands as described in Japji Sahib pauris 34–38. The lesson's descriptions of each are broadly accurate.

issues.claim_in_lesson: lust (kam), anger (krodh), greed (lobh), worldly attachment (moh) and pride (ahankar).
issues.verdict: Correct. These are the standard panj dosh (five vices/thieves) in Sikh teaching. The lesson's use of 'ahankar' for pride is standard; some sources list it as the fifth alongside haumai (ego), but combining them at GCSE level is acceptable.

issues.claim_in_lesson: karma in Sikhism is NOT fate or destiny imposed from outside. It is the natural consequence of a person's actions.
issues.verdict: Accurate distinction well-made. The lesson correctly flags this as a common misconception trap. No error.

findings.overall_lesson_verdict: PASS — no HIGH or MEDIUM issues. Five khands, panj dosh, gurmukh/manmukh distinction, karma/grace balance all correctly presented.

findings.lesson_title: The Oneness of Humanity and Equality

issues.claim_in_lesson: Guru Nanak's declaration 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' was a foundational statement of the equality of all people before God. He expressed this in practice by sitting and eating with people of all castes — a radical act in a deeply stratified society.
issues.verdict: Accurate. The tradition of eating with people of all backgrounds is supported in Janamsakhi literature. No error.

issues.category: Inclusion of non-Sikh composers in GGS
issues.claim_in_lesson: The scripture contains the writings not only of the Sikh Gurus but also of Muslim, Hindu and other composers from different castes and backgrounds — among them Kabir (a low-caste weaver), Sheikh Farid (a Muslim mystic) and Ravidas (a leatherworker considered among the lowest in caste hierarchy).
issues.verdict: Accurate. Kabir, Sheikh Farid (Baba Farid) and Ravidas/Ravidass are all genuine contributors to the GGS. Their caste descriptions are correct.

issues.category: Women and the Guru Granth Sahib — phrasing of GGS teaching
issues.claim_in_lesson: The Guru Granth Sahib asks why anyone should consider women inferior when it is women who give birth to the leaders, kings and prophets of the world.
issues.verdict: Accurate paraphrase of GGS Ang 473 (Guru Nanak, Raag Asa): 'From woman, man is born; within woman, man is conceived; to woman he is engaged and married. Woman becomes his friend; through woman, the future generations come. When his woman dies, he seeks another woman; to woman he is bound. So why call her bad? From her, kings are born.' Well-known verse; paraphrase in lesson is acceptable for GCSE.
issues.note: The lesson does not cite the Ang number here — acceptable at GCSE level but worth noting.

findings.overall_lesson_verdict: PASS — no HIGH or MEDIUM issues. Equality teaching, langar as expression of equality, Khalsa founding and Singh/Kaur naming all accurate.

issues.claim_in_lesson: Tan (physical sewa)... Man (mental sewa)... Dhan (material sewa)
issues.verdict: Correct. These three categories — tan, man, dhan — are the standard division found in Sikh teaching. No error.

issues.claim_in_lesson: Sikhs are encouraged to give a daswandh — a tenth of their income — in service, though this is a traditional expectation rather than a legal obligation.
issues.verdict: Accurate. Daswandh (dassond) = 'tenth portion'; giving a tenth of income is a traditional Sikh discipline. Correctly qualified as not a legal obligation.

findings.overall_lesson_verdict: PASS — no HIGH or MEDIUM issues. Sewa as worship (not charity), three forms, haumai/ego connection, sangat theology all accurate and well-explained.

issues.claim_in_lesson: a tall flagpole flying a triangular dark blue flag bearing the Khanda (the Sikh emblem)
issues.verdict: INACCURATE for mainstream UK gurdwaras. The traditional and most common Nishan Sahib is saffron/basanti (yellow-orange) in colour, not dark blue. Dark blue (surmai) is historically associated with the Nihang Sikh order. The Akal Takht issued a ruling in July 2024 mandating only basanti (yellow) or surmai (navy blue) — neither of which is specifically 'dark blue' as stated. Describing it as simply 'dark blue' without qualification is factually imprecise and will mislead students about what they will see outside a gurdwara in Britain.
issues.recommended_fix: Change to: 'a triangular saffron-coloured (or navy blue, depending on the gurdwara) flag bearing the Khanda.' Alternatively: 'a triangular flag — typically saffron, though some gurdwaras use dark blue — bearing the Khanda.'

issues.claim_in_lesson: The Guru Granth Sahib at GGS 305:4 emphasises the importance of prayer and remembrance of God in the home.
issues.verdict: Ang 305 falls within the Gauri raag section (Ang 151–346). The specific sub-verse notation ':4' is a plausible internal line reference used in some GGS indexing systems. Multiple AQA GCSE teaching resources cite 'GGS 305' in the context of home worship and the Nitnem, suggesting this is an accepted exam-board reference. The citation appears in the AQA specification context and is used on the AQA RS teaching site (williamsphysics.co.uk). No direct fabrication found, classified LOW.

issues.claim_in_lesson: The word gurdwara means 'doorway to the Guru' (from Punjabi: gur = Guru, dwara = door or gateway).
issues.verdict: Correct and standard definition. No error.

issues.category: Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha described as 'largest gurdwara outside India'
issues.claim_in_lesson: The largest is the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall, west London — the largest gurdwara outside India
issues.verdict: Widely stated in GCSE materials and general sources. Some sources contest this (the Gurdwara Sahib in Stockton, California and gurdwaras in Canada are also large), but the Southall claim is the standard AQA teaching position and commonly cited. No change needed at GCSE level.

findings.overall_lesson_verdict: NEAR-PASS — one MEDIUM issue (Nishan Sahib colour described as 'dark blue' when saffron is standard for mainstream UK gurdwaras). All other content — palki, takht, chauri, Darbar Sahib, langar description, sukhasan room — is accurate.

findings.lesson_title: Akhand Path, Langar and Nam Japna

issues.claim_in_lesson: It is the continuous, unbroken reading of the entire Guru Granth Sahib from beginning to end — all 1,430 pages. This takes approximately 48 hours.
issues.verdict: Correct. Standard Akhand Path duration is approximately 48 hours when recited in Gurmukhi. 1,430 angs confirmed. No error.

issues.claim_in_lesson: The institution of langar was established by Guru Nanak and developed through the ten Gurus. Guru Amar Das (the third Guru) made it mandatory for visitors to eat in the langar before seeking an audience with him.
issues.verdict: Partially accurate but requires nuance. The lesson correctly identifies Guru Nanak as the originator and Guru Amar Das as the Guru who formalised langar. However, multiple academic sources (Wikipedia, Britannica) indicate that Guru Angad (the second Guru) also significantly developed the langar institution — 'Guru Angad is notable for systematising the institution of langar in all Sikh gurdwara premises.' The lesson skips Guru Angad's contribution entirely, jumping from Guru Nanak to the third Guru. While the lesson isn't strictly wrong about Guru Amar Das making it mandatory, the omission of Guru Angad's role could confuse students who encounter exam sources crediting Angad with institutionalisation. Rated MEDIUM because the claim could produce a wrong attribution in an exam context.
issues.recommended_fix: Add: 'Guru Angad Dev (the second Guru) further systematised langar, and Guru Amar Das (the third Guru) made it mandatory...'

issues.claim_in_lesson: The Rehat Maryada (the Sikh code of conduct, formalised in 1945) confirms that the langar should be vegetarian.
issues.verdict: Correct. The Sikh Rehat Maryada was approved by the SGPC in 1945. Langar is confirmed as vegetarian in that code. No error.

issues.claim_in_lesson: one of the three pillars of Sikh teaching alongside honest work (kirat karni) and sharing with others (vand chakna).
issues.verdict: Correct. The three pillars — nam japna, kirat karni, vand chakna — are the standard formulation used in Sikh teaching and AQA materials.

findings.overall_lesson_verdict: NEAR-PASS — one MEDIUM issue (langar history skips Guru Angad's institutionalising role, creating a potential wrong-attribution risk). All other content — Akhand Path duration, Rehat Maryada date, nam japna mechanics, kirtan/ragis, Nitnem, Waheguru — is accurate.

issues.claim_in_lesson: Vaisakhi (also spelled Baisakhi) is celebrated in April and is one of the most important festivals in the Sikh calendar.
issues.verdict: Correct. Vaisakhi falls on 13 or 14 April annually in the Gregorian calendar. No error.

issues.category: Bandi Chhor Divas — number of princes
issues.claim_in_lesson: When the Emperor finally agreed to release him, Guru Hargobind refused to leave unless 52 Hindu princes who were also imprisoned were freed at the same time.
issues.verdict: Correct. Multiple sources confirm '52 rajas/princes' held at Gwalior Fort with Guru Hargobind, released under Emperor Jahangir. The detail about Guru Hargobind demanding their simultaneous release is accurate.

issues.claim_in_lesson: The sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, was imprisoned in Gwalior Fort by the Mughal Emperor Jahangir.
issues.verdict: Correct. Emperor Jahangir imprisoned Guru Hargobind at Gwalior Fort, c.1619. No error.

issues.claim_in_lesson: the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random, and the first letter of the first hymn on the left-hand page is read aloud by the granthi. The family chooses a name beginning with that letter.
issues.verdict: Accurate. Multiple authoritative sources (SikhiWiki, SikhNet) confirm the first letter used is from the top of the left-hand page of the randomly opened GGS. The lesson is correct. Downgraded from potential issue — no error found.

issues.claim_in_lesson: The Golden Temple (Harimandir Sahib — 'Temple of God') at Amritsar in Punjab is the most sacred site in Sikhism.
issues.verdict: INACCURATE translation. 'Harimandir' means 'House/Abode/Temple of God' — this part is fine. However the lesson also states in the Key Fact box that the temple 'was built under the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan Dev, and completed in 1604.' This is correct. The broader concern: the lesson does NOT mention that the pool of water around the Golden Temple (Amrit Sarovar — giving Amritsar its name) was created by the FOURTH Guru, Guru Ram Das, who also founded the city. The Golden Temple building itself was built under Guru Arjan Dev (fifth Guru). The lesson correctly attributes the building to Guru Arjan Dev but misses Guru Ram Das's founding role in the city and the pool.
issues.note: The claim about the building being completed under Guru Arjan Dev in 1604 is correct. The omission of Guru Ram Das as founder of Amritsar/the pool is a gap rather than a direct error, and won't produce wrong exam answers on the Golden Temple question specifically. However, the lesson correctly attributes everything it does state. Downgraded to MEDIUM (omission, not fabrication).
issues.recommended_fix: Add a sentence: 'The sacred pool (Amrit Sarovar) surrounding the Golden Temple was originally excavated by the fourth Guru, Guru Ram Das, who also founded the city of Amritsar.' This prevents confusion if students read that Guru Ram Das founded Amritsar in another lesson.

issues.claim_in_lesson: Unlike Hindu temples, the Golden Temple was built with four doors, one on each side, signifying that it is open to people from all four directions — a physical expression of the Sikh teaching that all are welcome regardless of caste, religion or background.
issues.verdict: Correct. The four-door design is confirmed as intentional by Guru Arjan Dev to symbolise openness to all directions/all people. Some sources also note the four doors represent the four traditional castes (varnas), symbolising that all are welcome — both interpretations are valid and the lesson's phrasing covers the main meaning accurately.

issues.category: Gurpurbs — Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur martyrdoms
issues.claim_in_lesson: Other major Gurpurbs include the birthday of Guru Gobind Singh and the martyrdom anniversaries of Guru Arjan Dev and Guru Tegh Bahadur (who were executed for refusing to convert to Islam — martyred for the right of religious freedom).
issues.verdict: Accurate on the martyrdom of Guru Arjan (fifth Guru, executed by Jahangir 1606) and Guru Tegh Bahadur (ninth Guru, executed by Aurangzeb 1675). The characterisation of both as being martyred for refusing to convert to Islam and defending religious freedom is a standard Sikh and AQA teaching position. No error.

findings.overall_lesson_verdict: NEAR-PASS — one MEDIUM omission (Guru Ram Das's founding of Amritsar/Amrit Sarovar not mentioned alongside the Golden Temple). All directly stated facts are accurate. Bandi Chhor Divas, Naam Karan, Gurpurbs, Vaisakhi all correctly described.

findings.lesson_title: Amrit Sanskar, the Khalsa and the Five Ks

issues.claim_in_lesson: On Vaisakhi in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh gathered thousands of Sikhs at Anandpur Sahib.
issues.verdict: Correct. The Khalsa was founded at Anandpur Sahib (specifically at the site of Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib) on Vaisakhi, 13 April 1699. No error.

issues.claim_in_lesson: five men — drawn from five different castes and regions of India — stepped forward.
issues.verdict: Correct. The five were from different castes/backgrounds: Daya Ram (Khatri, Lahore), Dharam Das (Jat, Hastinapur), Himmat Rai (waterman, Jagannath Puri), Mohkam Chand (washerman, Dwarka), Sahib Chand (barber, Bidar). Diverse castes and regions confirmed.

issues.category: Five Ks — all five named and described
issues.claim_in_lesson: Kesh (uncut hair), Kangha (wooden comb), Kara (steel bracelet), Kachera (cotton undergarment) and Kirpan (ceremonial sword).
issues.verdict: Correct. All five are accurately named and described. Spelling 'Kangha' (vs 'Kanga') is a minor variant — both are accepted. 'Kachera' vs 'Kachhera' is also a minor variant; the lesson's spelling is standard in AQA materials. No material error.

issues.category: Amrit Sanskar — steel bowl and sugar crystals
issues.claim_in_lesson: the Panj Pyare prepare the amrit — a mixture of water and sugar crystals (patasas) — in a steel bowl (bata) while stirring it with a double-edged sword (khanda)
issues.verdict: Correct. Patasas (sugar crystals/plums), bata (steel bowl), khanda (double-edged sword) — all confirmed by multiple sources including SikhiWiki and Amrit Sanskar Wikipedia article. However the lesson says 'reciting hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib' while sources specify five banis are recited (Japji Sahib, Jaap Sahib, Sawayae, Chaupai Sahib, Anand Sahib — some from Dasam Granth). The lesson's phrasing 'hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib' is slightly imprecise (two of the five banis come from the Dasam Granth) but acceptable simplification for GCSE.

issues.claim_in_lesson: Guru Gobind Singh gave all Sikh men the name Singh (meaning 'lion') and all Sikh women the name Kaur (meaning 'princess').
issues.verdict: Correct. Singh = lion; Kaur = princess/prince. These are the standard meanings used in Sikh tradition and AQA materials. No error.

issues.claim_in_lesson: Kirpan symbolises the duty to defend the weak and stand for justice — not aggression or violence. It reflects the Khalsa's commitment to sant-sipahi: the 'saint-soldier' ideal, combining spiritual devotion (sant) with the courage to defend others (sipahi).
issues.verdict: Correct. Sant-sipahi is confirmed as a core Sikh concept, first endorsed by Guru Hargobind and solidified by Guru Gobind Singh. The characterisation of kirpan as defensive (for others) rather than aggressive is accurate per Sikh teaching.

findings.overall_lesson_verdict: PASS — no HIGH or MEDIUM issues. All five Ks correctly listed and described. Khalsa founding date, location, Panj Pyare diversity, Amrit Sanskar ceremony mechanics, amritdhari/sahajdhari distinction all accurate.

lessons_with_issues: 5147a507 — The Gurdwara: Worship and Community (MEDIUM: Nishan Sahib described as dark blue; saffron is standard for UK gurdwaras)
07cdf80f — Akhand Path, Langar and Nam Japna (MEDIUM: langar history skips Guru Angad Dev's institutionalising role between Nanak and Amar Das)
39be2f8f — Festivals, Birth and Naming Ceremonies (MEDIUM: Golden Temple section omits Guru Ram Das founding Amritsar/Amrit Sarovar)

top_3_worst_lessons.reason: Describes the Nishan Sahib as 'dark blue' — this is wrong for mainstream UK gurdwaras where the flag is saffron. Students visiting any of the 250+ UK gurdwaras will see a saffron flag; being told it is dark blue is a directly testable factual error. Students citing 'dark blue' in exam answers about the gurdwara may lose marks.

top_3_worst_lessons.lesson_title: Akhand Path, Langar and Nam Japna
top_3_worst_lessons.reason: Langar history jumps from Guru Nanak (founder) directly to Guru Amar Das (third Guru) institutionalising it, omitting Guru Angad Dev (second Guru) who also systematised langar. AQA mark schemes may reward mention of multiple Gurus' roles; a student who has only learned this lesson could be caught out by a source crediting Guru Angad.

The Golden Temple section attributes the building to Guru Arjan Dev (correct) but never mentions that the pool (Amrit Sarovar) and the city of Amritsar were founded by Guru Ram Das (fourth Guru). This is a gap that creates cross-lesson confusion — the lesson on practices repeatedly references the Golden Temple and Amritsar but a student could not explain Amritsar's name or its founding from this lesson alone.
